devpost_page.title: Formly - the secure, fast form filler
devpost_page.tagline: Formly is Stripe for forms: click “Fill with Formly,” connect accounts like Google Drive, and Formly fills the business’s blank form for you. They get a finished form; your raw data stays private.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every signup, application and checkout asks for the same things: your name, address, ID, income, car, emergency contact. We type them again and again, often from documents we already have sitting in Google Drive or iCloud. Browser autofill only covers a handful of basic fields and stops at anything like an SSN, a driver's license number or a VIN. Businesses feel it too, because every extra minute on a long form is a chance for someone to give up. We wanted something like Stripe Checkout, but for forms: one button a business can drop in, that fills the whole form from the user's own data, while the user stays in control of exactly what gets shared.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: A business adds a Fill with Formly button to its form. When you press it, a secure Formly window opens, and: You connect your data once. Upload files (PDFs, photos, Word docs, text, zip folders), or sign in with Google or iCloud to pull in your profile, contacts, email receipts, Drive or iCloud Drive documents, Apple Wallet and your Health Medical ID. Formly builds your digital twin. It reads everything and keeps a private, organized profile of the facts forms ask for, each one linked back to the file it came from. You can edit any fact or mark it as never shared. Formly fills the form. It matches your twin to the business's questions and fills what it can. If something isn't in your data, it leaves the field blank instead of guessing. You review and approve. Every answer shows where it came from. Sensitive details like your SSN, IDs and card numbers need an explicit yes, and you choose between being asked or sharing automatically. The business gets only the approved answers. Your files never leave Formly. It also handles open-ended questions. On a job application, it drafts short answers in your own voice from your actual resume, and it refuses to make up experience you don't have. To show it working, we built four realistic demo forms styled after the real businesses: a T-Mobile switch and plan signup, a SpaceXAI job application, a Chase Freedom Unlimited card application and a California DMV vehicle title and registration form. Nine made-up people, each with full documents

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: App: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS 4, with SQLite for local storage of sources, the twin, permissions and fill sessions. Gemini API: Gemini does all of Formly's reading and writing, through Google's @google/genai SDK. Reading files: we send PDFs and photos (like a driver's license) straight to Gemini as inline files, and it transcribes every detail into text. Word files are converted locally, with no AI call needed. Building the twin: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite merges all of a person's sources into one organized profile, and in parallel pulls out typed key facts, each tagged with its source and how sensitive it is. Filling forms: every fill uses Gemini's structured output. We give it a JSON schema, so it can only return a value, a source and a confidence for fields that actually exist on the form. Writing short answers: Gemini 3.5 Flash writes these, since writing quality matters more there than speed. Speed and reliability: we run Gemini with low thinking, which made fills several times faster with the same accuracy on these tasks. If a model is overloaded or rate limited, the request automatically retries on the next Gemini model. Test data: Gemini also generated the realistic email inboxes for our synthetic test people. Backup: with an Anthropic key set, every request can run on Claude instead, using the same prompts. Pipeline: files become text, which then becomes the digital twin. Gemini API looks at the form's fields and fills it in with the Digital Twin'

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Getting gigabytes of data into a form, fast. A person's data can run to gigabytes of photos, PDFs, documents and email, and nobody will wait minutes for a form. Sending all of it to a model on every fill would be slow and expensive. So Formly does the heavy reading once, when you connect your data: Gemini transcribes each file a single time and distills everything into a compact digital twin. A fill then only sends that small profile and the form's field list, so it comes back in a few seconds. Building the twin and filling the form each run two Gemini calls in parallel, and low thinking plus structured output kept every call short. Made-up answers. Sometimes it would hallucinate information, so we implemented a fact checking algorithm. Missing data. Google sync first skipped key documents, so some important details were never synced to the Digital Twin Free tier limits. We added automatic fallbacks between Gemini models.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: From one Google or iCloud connection, Formly fills every field on all four demo forms. On our synthetic test set, it got 107 of 108 field checks right. When the data doesn't support an answer, including a written one, Formly leaves it blank. By default, SSNs, IDs and card numbers always ask first, while basic details fill without interruptions. The demo forms look and behave like the real T-Mobile, SpaceXAI, Chase and DMV flows.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Teaching Formly not to answer was difficult. Sometimes we needed no answer, and it would give us hallucinated information. Reading data once, up front, matters more for speed than faster model calls.

sections.heading: What's next for Formly - the secure, fast form filler
sections.text: Real Google and Apple sign-in, plus banks and more data sources. An SDK and browser extension so Formly works on any form. Encrypting the digital twin on your device.

devpost_page.title: Brawlmegle
devpost_page.tagline: Omegle was for talking to strangers. Omoggle was for mogging them. Now there’s Brawlmegle: create your fighter and punch, block, and dodge your way through camera-powered battles with friends.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: The developers of this project grew up on Wii Sports boxing and gesturing in front of Xbox Kinect. Next came VR boxing but to us, it felt like it was missing something. With Brawlmegle, we mixed old with new, added the omph which VR Boxing lacks, the effect and impact that classic fighting games, Street Fighter and Tekken, gives.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Brawlmegle is a webcam fighting game where you fight as yourself: Get scanned: stand in front of your laptop camera, and in about 40 seconds our own GPU server turns you into a stylized, rigged 3D fighter. You can even watch it form live. Throw hands: punch, hook, uppercut, block, duck, dodge, kick. The camera reads what you meant to do, and the fight engine decides what actually happens in order to create an awesome strategic and visual experience. And of course it has the flashy arcade stuff we all love like hero entrances, VS screens, and even live AI commentary powered by ElevenLabs.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The game is React, TypeScript, and Three.js in the browser, so there's nothing to install. Body tracking happens via Google's MediaPipe and runs in a Web Worker at around 30 frames per second. Our secret sauce is the intent reader. Instead of mapping your skeleton onto the model, it watches your motion and decides "that was a right hook". The game is online peer-to-peer via WebRTC, with a small matchmaking server and relay hosted on a tiny AWS EC2 instance. The fight engine runs on one of the laptops: it acts as the referee, and the other one just mirrors it and collects input from the second player. For the fighters, we built our own "forge": GPT writes your fighter's backstory and draws a character sheet from your scan. TRELLIS.2, an open-source 3D model we run on our own AWS GPU, sculpts it into a 3D fighter in seconds. Our own Blender auto-rigger gives it a skeleton so it can actually fight. A last step paints your face back on, so it looks a little more recognizable. We were also fortunate to have a talented Blender wizard on our team, who built an incredible Mount Rainier arena so you're fighting right here in the PNW.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest challenge was the intent reader. We kept having issues with fake moves, wrong moves, and even huge delays, which defeated the dream of building something punchy. But as we kept recording fights and running tests, we were able to tune a config system that we believe got to a point where the gameplay is actually fun. The other big one was the 3D fighters. Our 3D generation provider ran out of credits mid-hackathon, so we spun up our own GPU server, which ended up faster. Then the models came out hollow, so dresses and hoodies broke the rigging, and we had to write our own rig checker and fixes until every fighter worked.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Witnessing going from webcam scan to a playable 3D version of yourself in under a minute never gets old. Real fighting-game feel from just a camera: combos, counters, guard breaks Omegle-style matchmaking with live cameras, fully peer-to-peer An AI live commentator that's actually aware of what's going on in the game.

sections.text: Agent Builder - Conversational AI Workflow Platform

sections.heading: 🎯 Inspiration
sections.text: The inspiration for Agent Builder came from a simple observation: building AI agent workflows is incredibly powerful but unnecessarily complex. Data scientists and developers spend countless hours writing boilerplate code, configuring integrations, and manually wiring together agents and tools—time that could be better spent on solving actual business problems. We envisioned a world where anyone could describe what they want in plain English and watch a production-ready AI workflow materialize before their eyes. We were particularly inspired by the democratization potential of NVIDIA's NIM ecosystem. The combination of powerful reasoning models like llama-3.1-nemotron-nano-8B-v1 and efficient retrieval embeddings like nv-embedqa-e5-v5 opened up possibilities for truly intelligent workflow generation—not just template filling, but genuine understanding of user intent and intelligent component selection. We wanted to prove that with the right architecture, AI could not only understand what you want to build but actually build it for you.

sections.heading: 💡 What it does
sections.text: Agent Builder is a conversational AI workflow platform that transforms natural language descriptions into fully deployable agent workflows. Instead of dragging, dropping, and configuring nodes manually, users simply chat with an AI assistant that understands their requirements and generates complete workflows automatically. devpost_page.tagline: OncoBot, a Discord bot that uses computer vision to detect signs of melanoma from submitted images of suspicious skin lesions and integrates a map API to guide patients to nearby health facilities.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Seeing the growing number of cancer patients around the world and with two of our team members having multiple family members directly affected by the disease, we thought of making a bot that can preemptively help detect skin cancer at its early stages so that people can get the desired treatment. Annually, around 200,000 individuals globally are diagnosed with melanoma, and despite rapid advances in oncological treatment, many find out too late. This inspired us to design OncoBot as a way to help worried individuals check for skin cancer.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: OncoBot allows patients to inspect suspicious marks on their skin and directs them to nearby medical services. Using computer vision, the program detects the presence of melanoma from the images that the user inputs. It utilizes various image processing techniques to remove noise from images and try to find potentially dangerous lesions. Additionally, the bot uses a Google Maps API to navigate the user to their nearest 5 hospitals for further examination if they type in an address.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The project was built entirely using Python, as it allowed for the easiest integration of computer vision libraries, as well as Discord and map APIs. We had one team focused on the computer vision aspect, developing the algorithm and image processing sequence. This was crucial, as each step needs to be in the right order so that important information was preserved. This part involved much exploration, as only one of our members had prior experience with the OpenCV library. Our second team was focused on creating the user experience, integrating the bot using the Discord API and enabling it to access geographical data to find nearby medical services using a Google Maps API.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We faced many significant problems through the course of this project. As this the first hackathon for all of us and none of us are particularly experienced with programming projects, the brainstorming process was uniquely challenging. Working within the constraints of our respective skillsets was something we had to pay close attention to so that no one would be unable to contribute. Another problem we faced was the privacy of the virtual environment on the GitHub repository for the project. The environment included the unique token for the bot, which was called by the "main.py" file. This was a problem, as publicizing the token was not an option. We inevitably realized that this token was not meant to be published. Other users, should they want to replicate the functionality of the bot, should make their own bot with its own token and replicate the rest of the code; otherwise, they are able to join the server with our bot. Obvious in hindsight, but we were stumped nonetheless. The most pressing problem we had was near the end of the project, as merging all parts of the project produced many errors apropos recognition of dependencies. After pulling the CV algorithm onto the computer with the Discord bot, the interpreter was throwing false errors for nearly every library that had been installed, saying that it couldn't recognize them. Despite these errors, the program ended up running exactly as intended, but we still don't know why those errors came up, whether or not they'r

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We accomplished many feats that we didn't even fathom at the start of the project. First, on the CV algorithm, we were able to achieve a cumulative 82% accurate labeling system using solely existing pre-trained models within OpenCV. Due to both technical and technological limitations for us, training a model would not have been feasible, so getting close to what a neural network trained from scratch specifically on this datatset might be able to achieve is something we're incredibly proud of. Beyond that, though, we're proud of our ability to work as a team to see a project to completion. Each one of us has experience starting coding projects that often end up unfinished, so actually having a collaborative effort with multiple moving parts and functionalities we were unfamiliar with end up with something tangible is an amazing feeling for all four of us.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This experience was, more than anything else, an amazing learning experience. We all obviously became much more familiar with the tools we were using for our individual part of the project. But there was a constant cross-pollination; the CV team learned about all the parts of the Discord and Google Maps API integration (especially during the final hours-long dependency issue) and vice versa. We all also became familiar with the development process itself, including key components such as GitHub functionalities, how virtual environments work and why they're useful, and more general skills of teamwork, time management, and communication. It was overall an extremely fulfilling 36 hours that's going to have an impact on all our programming lives for the foreseeable future.

sections.heading: What's next for OncoBot
sections.text: We think that OncoBot can be made even more effective in the future with more extensive capabilities and features. We plan on further refining the CV aspect by training our own model on the specific datatset so that it's more targeted to images of skin, rather than images of anything. Additionally, we'd like to extend it's usage so that it can also detect other skin conditions such as eczema or carcinoma, allowing some sort of future integration with virtual healthcare platforms so that the patients can also directly connect to healthcare professionals for an immediate diagnosis. Most importantly, we would like OncoBot to be a free to use, accessible platform for all people to get instant medical advice and guidance when care might otherwise be immediately available.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We all see the signs: a new condo, a townhouse complex, a high-rise. Most people walk by with a lingering question: How will this actually impact our community during construction and long after? MapD turns that concern into clarity.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: MapD is a geospatial storytelling platform that translates fragmented open data into a single, understandable view of an urban project. Drop a pin (or paste a permit address) and MapD: Aggregates relevant public datasets (permits, zoning, transit, 311/service requests, and more). Normalizes & links records to the same place and time windows. Summarizes likely impacts (traffic, noise, accessibility, nearby amenities) into plain language. Visualizes changes with a clean, minimal map.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: 24-hour goals Ship a deployed MVP Prioritize unity & clarity over flash Engage our community with approachable language Frontend: Vite + React + Tailwind for a unified, minimalist UI/UX (Mapbox GL for interactive layers). Backend: Python + FastAPI with MongoDB for schema-light ingestion, all containerized via Docker Compose. Intelligence: OpenAI-assisted parsing to reconcile messy fields (addresses, parcel IDs, neighborhood names) and to generate concise, non-technical summaries. Infra: Vercel (frontend) + DigitalOcean (API) + MongoDB, with Cloudflare Workers bridging edge routing and caching.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: No common standards across open datasets. Address formats, IDs, and time fields varied wildly. We built a reconciliation layer (geocoding + fuzzy matching) to align records. Concurrent cleaning and embedding. We needed embeddings early for entity linking while cleansing was still in flight; we solved this with staged, idempotent jobs. Token efficiency at scale. devpost_page.title: YGroove
devpost_page.tagline: YGroove is an interactive app that guides users through precise movements for physical therapy, dance, and fitness, using real-time pose tracking to offer personalized feedback and enhancements.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Have you ever wished you could ensure your movements are executed correctly and align perfectly? Whether it's performing an exercise with impeccable form, stretching effectively for physical therapy, or executing the sharpest moves on the dance floor, we all want to shine in the spotlight. We're driven by the transformative potential of precise movement, recognizing its impact on physical health and artistic expression. By equipping individuals with tools for refinement, we aim to foster confidence, self-expression, and overall well-being. Our mission is to democratize access to movement education, enabling everyone to embrace the joy of fluid, precise movement. In our journey, we strive to break down barriers, making sure that cutting-edge movement analysis is not just a luxury for the few. With our platform, even those without immediate access to gyms, dance studios, or rehabilitation centers can enhance their movements and technique. We want to bring the dance studio and the therapist's expertise into every living room, ensuring inclusivity and the opportunity for personal growth. We envision a world where every step, stretch, and stance leads you closer to perfection, whether on TikTok's virtual stage, in a yoga studio, or the comfort of your home.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: We created an interactive web tool that computationally assesses user movements and scores how similar they are to a reference video (e.g. a video of a person dancing, or doing an exercise, etc). Users can then either upload a video of themselves or use our live webcam feature to assess their movements compared to those of expert physical therapists, fitness instructors, or dancers for any music. These templates cover a wide range of activities from dance to fitness routines to therapeutic exercises. Users are provided with a graph showing their performance and how closely they match the reference video over time. Our system not only matches users' movements to these standards but also provides areas of improvement and personalized recommendations to help users refine their techniques. Our live webcam feature even allows users to follow the reference video in real-time and receive feedback.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: React & Next.js for the frontend Node.js for the backend TensorFlow (MoveNet model) for pose estimation Dynamic Time Wrapping algorithm for scoring. Our application leverages a React & Next.js front-end, providing a user-friendly interface that's hosted on Vercel for effortless deployment and scalability. The backbone of our back end is Node.js, which manages data processing and integrates seamlessly with our core technologies for movement analysis. A critical component of our system is TensorFlow, specifically utilized for our deployment of the MoveNet pose estimation model. This model enables us to accurately detect and track keypoints of the user's movements in real-time, forming the foundation of our interactive feedback system. Once poses are estimated, we use this data to dynamically render key points on the user interface, visually guiding users to align their movements with predefined expert patterns. Further refining our analysis, we employ Dynamic Time Warping, an algorithm for aligning temporal sequences and comparing their similarity. This allows us to measure how closely a user's movements match with our expert templates. By quantifying movement accuracy, we can provide users with specific performance scores and insights, highlighting areas of excellence and those needing improvement. We also use sliding window techniques to identify these areas of the user's movement that are misaligned with the reference video.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We encountered challenges in real-time pose tracking, addressing latency issues when translating Python models to JavaScript, and implementing the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm. For example an initial problem we faced was: in our React app, when the user uploads a video and we want to extract the poses from the video, each frame would only be fetched when the video was playing in the background. Thus, extracting poses from a 40 second video would take 40 seconds. We found a solution to process frames quickly, and only focus on the specific frames that we were interested in (doing pose detection at 5 fps). We also had to improve the efficiency of our frame processing code and use Promises to make sure that 2 videos could have their poses extracted at the same time, reducing the amount of delay before getting back results. There were also issues with state variables, and normalizing/calculating user keypoint coordinates and scores.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud of achieving full-scale posture tracking and integrating advanced backend algorithms. Our success in building this sophisticated platform within 24 hours stands as a testament to our commitment and the power of collaboration.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Throughout the development process, we've gained a deeper understanding of posture tracking capabilities using Tensorflow, optimized algorithms for real-time data processing (particularly from a live webcam), parallelizing inferencing tasks, and harnessing the power of webcams for capturing and analyzing user movements.

sections.heading: What's next for YGroove
sections.text: Looking ahead, we plan to expand our library of movements, integrate with more comprehensive health data, and explore machine learning models that can predict and correct movement patterns. Our goal is to become the go-to platform for anyone looking to perfect their movements, whether for health, fitness, or the sheer joy of dancing. Additionally, we'd like to build a social aspect to the app where users can easily share a "challenge" link of themself following the movements of a reference video (e.g. a new dance or exercise routine) and other people can click on the link, and take their own shot at performing the movements, with a leaderboard showing the top users who matched most closely to the reference. Thereby, this ignites friendly competition and encourages people to engage socially and physically.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Between credit cards, memberships, and loyalty programs, we all collect benefits faster than we use them. Every store wants you to join its rewards program. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Congratulations: you now have another coupon to forget about. VISA found that consumers hold an average of 17.4 loyalty memberships but actively use only 8.8. In fact, Americans miss out on up to $10 billion in loyalty savings every year ! People are signing up for rewards, earning benefits, and then forgetting they ever existed! So we built Lapse: a browser extension that remembers your rewards and does the checkout math for you, because we're obsessed with our customers.

sections.heading: Innovation
sections.text: It finds coupons, checks your coupons, memberships, and credit card benefits to find the best combination that gives our customers the best deal. We call this "stacking". Lapse also keeps track of what’s about to expire , so a reward you meant to “save for later” will be pushed to the front of the stack so you'll actually get a chance to use it before it's gone. Expiration-aware search brings those offers forward, while checkout recommendations prioritize savings. Lapse does the math for you. Minimum spends, exclusions, and cashback rates all affect the answer, so we built a constraint model using Google’s OR-Tools solver to handle the math.

sections.heading: User Experience
sections.text: Lapse finds your rewards while you shop. Your dashboard keeps the coupons, expiration dates, and savings in one place. We chose an extension because people already have somewhere to shop, and our extension is a friendly aid to save people time, money, and maximize the benefits they already have. Our LapseSense notice brings relevant benefits into that shopping experience. Live updates arrive through server-sent events, so a newly received reward can appear without a manual refresh. A reward alert needs a recognizable identity across very different shopping pages, which is why we went with a brutalist style UI. Bold colors, thick outlines, and our brutalist visual direction make Lapse feel distinct and unique. On the dashboard, individual rewards look like real little coupons to add a fun touch.

sections.heading: How We Stand Out
sections.text: Lapse connects your personal offers to the cart in front of you. That means checking eligibility, comparing combinations, selecting a payment card, and recording the resulting savings. Our custom merchant tags and term-to-category map also help connect everyday shopping language to rewards. So, searching for “shoes” should not need to remember the exact wording of a footwear email. The distinction is the decision process. A large discount can block another benefit. A smaller compatible offer can produce a better result. An impressive cashback rate can be irrelevant at the wrong merchant. Lapse puts those conditions into the calculation.

sections.text: Fireline Tagline: Satellites see a wildfire once it is big. Fireline sees the first smoke.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: From January 1 to April 13, 2025, the Florida Forest Service counted 1,300 wildfires and 57,025 acres burned ( FOX 35 ). Much of that land is remote: no power lines, no cell signal, nobody watching. Satellites can't close that gap on their own. The ones sharp enough to see a small fire pass over a few times a day: VIIRS has about 375 m pixels and 3 to 4 looks a day at mid-latitudes ( NASA Earthdata ). Ground cameras see smoke sooner, but they need a tower, grid power and an internet connection. We wanted a camera box you can strap to a tree in the middle of nowhere that decides on its own whether it is seeing smoke, and that sends only what matters.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Fireline is a flock of tree-mounted camera units and a live console for the crew that manages them. Each unit runs a smoke detection model on its own NVIDIA Jetson, wakes up only when the weather says fire is likely, and sends a single alert packet of 340 bytes or less over a satellite link. The console puts every unit on a map and sounds the alarm the moment one of them confirms smoke. Smoke detection on the device: Pyronear's open YOLO smoke model runs on the Jetson's GPU. Smoke must appear in at least 4 of the last 6 frames, which filters out clouds, fog and dust. Weather-gated wake-up: a cheap humidity sensor on an ESP32 sets a fire-risk tier. The Jetson scans every 30 minutes when it's humid, every 5 minutes when it's drying out, and continuously in critical fire weather. Satellite-sized alerts: every message fits the 340-byte limit of an Iridium short burst data message. In our tests a smoke event is 178 bytes. Images never cross the satellite link. A live console: a fleet map with markers colored by state, an alarm and desktop notification that fly the map to the unit, weather charts for each unit, and a link log showing each packet's size and satellite delay. Plain-language write-ups: each incident gets an instant summary ("Smoke seen by gw-14 in 5 of 6 frames during critical fire weather (34 °C, 22 % humidity). Likely early wildfire."), which Gemma 3 then rewrites for the crew. Gemma also gives a second opinion on the smoke crop. The demo: we point a hair dryer at th

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: DHT11 → ESP32 sets the fire-risk tier → MQTT wakes the Jetson → smoke model + 4-of-6 frame check → interest score → 340-byte packet over the simulated satellite link → FastAPI on Azure → WebSocket → every open console Field unit (hardware) NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano runs the smoke model on its GPU with TensorRT , through Ultralytics . It idles with the model loaded until the ESP32 asks for a scan. ESP32 (Arduino) is the always-on sentry. It reads a DHT11 , averages 3 readings, changes tier only after 3 agreeing readings, and drives the status LED and buzzer. MQTT with a Mosquitto broker on the Jetson connects the two inside the box. AI/ML Pyronear's YOLO wildfire smoke model from Hugging Face (Apache 2.0), trained on Pyro-SDIS, a dataset of labelled smoke images from fixed ground cameras. No training needed. An interest score: average confidence × (frames with smoke / 6) × fire-weather weight . Smoke in critical weather outranks a faint blob on a humid day. An alert fires at 0.5. Gemma 3 (4B) served by Ollama writes each incident up and checks the smoke crop. Backend and infrastructure FastAPI + SQLite ground station: a satellite simulator (340-byte limit, 5–20 s delay, optional drops), incident grouping, offline detection, and a WebSocket for live updates. Azure VM running Docker Compose : the app, Gemma on Ollama, and Caddy for automatic HTTPS (browsers only allow notifications on secure sites). Frontend React , TypeScript and Vite , with Leaflet for the map on Esri satellite

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: A satellite link delivers out of order. With a 5–20 s random delay, an older heartbeat can land after a newer one. The ground station only lets the newest packet set a unit's state. It treats a packet as a duplicate only when the unit, counter and timestamp all match, because a rebooted unit restarts its counter. 340 bytes is a tight budget. We used short keys and rounded numbers, and kept images off the satellite link entirely. The unit refuses to send anything over the limit. A Jetson is slow to boot. Power-cycling it for every scan wasn't practical, so the cheap ESP32 does the always-on watching and the Jetson stays idle with the model loaded until it's needed. AI write-ups on a CPU-only server. Gemma on a CPU VM can take a while. The console shows a template summary instantly, and Gemma's version replaces it when it arrives. If Gemma never answers, the alert still works. We changed the architecture mid-build. We started with a Raspberry Pi ground station and an installed desktop app, and merged them into one hosted website. That meant fewer devices at the judging table, and anyone on the crew can open the console.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Detection never leaves the forest. The decision "is this smoke?" happens on the box. Only a small verdict crosses the satellite link, which answers the reason ground cameras need towers and internet today. The whole chain, end to end: weather sensor, wake-up, on-device detection, satellite-sized uplink, live alert on the map. A console built for the crew, not the demo. Alerts group into incidents, units that go quiet turn grey, and every packet's size and delay is on screen. Honest about what's real. The satellite link and most of the fleet are simulated, and the console labels every simulated unit on screen.

devpost_page.title: Eco Fast Track
devpost_page.tagline: A smart water management tool that helps households and property managers optimize water usage, save on utilities, and promote conservation through personalized insights and community-driven data.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: After conducting research on the primary expenses faced by property managers, we identified faulty water gauges as a significant issue. Property managers often depend on tenants to report problems or must coordinate inconvenient check-ins to identify issues. To address this, we developed an intuitive web application designed to streamline the process, allowing property managers to proactively manage water usage without awkward tenant interactions. At the same time, tenants gain an engaging, community-focused experience that promotes sustainability. Drawing inspiration from the popularity of visually appealing and personalized data presentations, we aimed to create a solution that’s both practical and fun—combining functionality with a touch of a "Spotify Wrapped" vibe to make data meaningful and enjoyable.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our tool uses smart gauge sensors to monitor water temperature and flow, providing real-time insights into usage. It aggregates data over time, compares it to global benchmarks, and uses AI to offer personalized water-saving recommendations. Property managers can proactively address inefficiencies, while tenants receive automated email alerts if their usage exceeds the average. With an optional community-sharing feature and engaging, user-friendly visuals, the platform promotes accountability, sustainability, and collaboration.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Using the IoT grover kit (specifically the temperature, potentiometer, and an LCD) as our smart gauge sensor to provide the data to a webpage via serial. On the software end python, Node.Js, Gemini, Pinata, and Next.Js are used to give tenants personal advice based on their own sensor aggregations and for plot development.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Originally planning to use wifi module however a successful connection was very rare Spent 3 hours trying to get the LCD to turn on and it turned out being due to an incompatible arduino board with the grove kit. 3D printed encasement did not fit all components so there was a bit of improvising there.
